quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: The first words of fabric design, from shedding to twill.

questions.q: The three primary motions of a loom, in order, are
questions.explain: The shed opens, the weft is inserted, and the reed beats the pick into the cloth.

questions.q: Shedding is
options: Pushing the pick against the cloth
Dividing the warp into two sheets to make an opening for the weft
Winding the cloth on the roller
questions.explain: Some ends are lifted and others lowered. Which ends lift on which pick is the weave.

questions.q: On point paper, each vertical column of squares stands for
questions.explain: Columns are ends and rows are picks, with the first pick at the bottom.

questions.q: A filled square on point paper means
options: The weft passes over the end
The warp end is lifted over that pick
questions.explain: Filled = warp up, so warp shows on the face at that point.

questions.q: The repeat of a weave is
options: The number of healds on the loom
The smallest block of ends and picks that tiles the whole cloth
The number of picks per inch
questions.explain: Plain weave repeats on 2 ends × 2 picks; a 3/1 twill on 4 × 4.

questions.q: Which shedding mechanism controls every warp end individually?
questions.explain: A jacquard lifts each end by its own hook, so large figured designs are possible.

questions.q: Let-off and take-up are the motions that keep weaving continuous by feeding warp and winding cloth.
questions.explain: They are the secondary motions that accompany shedding, picking and beating-up.

questions.q: In a “2/1” twill, the figures mean that each end is
options: In two colours and one weave
questions.explain: The numbers are the lifting order of one end: two up, one down.

questions.q: A Z twill is one whose diagonal
questions.explain: Like the middle stroke of the letter Z, the line rises to the right; an S twill rises to the left.

questions.q: GSM is the weight in grams of one square metre of fabric.
questions.explain: It is the usual way of stating fabric weight; ounces per square yard is GSM ÷ 33.9.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: How construction, mechanism and weave depend on one another.

questions.q: A design needs 12 different end movements. Which is the simplest mechanism that can weave it?
questions.explain: Tappets handle about 6–8 frames; a dobby controls 14–20 or more, enough for 12.

questions.q: The repeat of a regular twill written 3/1 is
questions.explain: The repeat is the sum of the numbers, 3 + 1 = 4, on both ends and picks.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is called balanced because
options: Warp and weft show equally on the face
It weighs the same in warp and weft
questions.explain: Each end is up for two picks and down for two, so face and back look alike.

questions.q: Turn a 3/1 warp-faced twill over. The back shows
questions.explain: What is warp-up on the face is warp-down on the back, so the back is the weft-faced 1/3 twill.

questions.q: A pointed twill drafted 1-2-3-4-3-2 has a repeat of 6 ends. It needs
questions.explain: Ends that move alike share a heald. Ends 5 and 6 repeat the movement of ends 3 and 2.

questions.q: If the picks per inch of a cloth are raised and nothing else changes, the fabric becomes
questions.explain: More picks mean more weft yarn per square metre.

questions.q: Plain weave can be woven on a tappet loom.
questions.explain: It needs only two different end movements, well within a tappet’s capacity.

questions.q: The quick rule GSM ≈ (EPI ÷ Ne warp + PPI ÷ Ne weft) × 25 gives a higher weight when
options: The counts are coarser or the threads denser
questions.explain: Dividing by a smaller Ne (coarser yarn) or having more threads per inch both raise the result.

questions.q: A steep twill differs from a regular twill in that its diagonal
options: Rises at a steeper angle, such as 63°
questions.explain: Cavalry twill is the lecture’s example of a steep, 63° twill with a bold double ridge.

questions.q: A large floral pattern in which every end moves differently can be woven on a dobby loom.
questions.explain: A dobby is limited by its number of heald frames. Independent control of every end needs a jacquard.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting on point paper and working out constructions.

questions.q: A cloth has 96 ends per inch and is 58 inches wide. How many ends are in the warp?
Use the quick rule to estimate the GSM of 30 × 30 / 76 × 68, to the nearest whole number.
A fabric weighs 170 GSM. What is that in ounces per square yard, to two decimals? (divide by 33.9)
questions.explain: 170 ÷ 33.9 = 5.01 oz per square yard.

questions.q: How many ends are there in one repeat of a 2/1 twill?
questions.explain: The repeat is the sum of the figures: 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: In one repeat of a 3/1 twill (4 ends × 4 picks), how many of the 16 squares on point paper are filled?
questions.explain: Each end is up on 3 of the 4 picks: 3 × 4 = 12 filled squares.

questions.q: How many heald frames does a 2/2 twill need with a straight draft?
questions.explain: Its four ends all move differently, so it needs 4 healds.

questions.q: A cloth must have 60 picks per inch when finished and contracts 8% in length after the loom. How many picks per inch are set on the loom, to one decimal?
questions.explain: 60 × 0.92 = 55.2 picks per inch on the loom.

questions.q: A twill is written 2/1/1/2. How many ends are in its repeat?
questions.explain: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6 ends (and picks).

questions.q: A warp has 4,000 ends and the warp yarn is 9% longer than the cloth. How many yards of warp yarn are in one yard of cloth?
In a 2/2 twill, how many picks does each warp float pass over?
questions.explain: Each end is up for 2 picks, then down for 2.

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: A drill is to be reproduced from a buyer’s sample: construction, weight and loom set-up.

questions.q: How many ends are in the warp?
How many picks per inch must be set on the loom, to one decimal?
How many yards of warp yarn are needed for one yard of cloth, to the nearest yard?
Estimate the weight in GSM with the quick rule, to the nearest whole number.
What is that weight in ounces per square yard, to one decimal? (GSM ÷ 33.9)
questions.explain: 253.75 ÷ 33.9 = 7.5 oz per square yard.

questions.q: What is the repeat of the weave?
questions.explain: 3 + 1 = 4, so the repeat is 4 ends × 4 picks.

questions.q: With a straight draft, how many heald frames are needed, and which mechanism is enough?
questions.explain: Four different end movements need four frames, which a tappet (cam) loom handles easily.

questions.q: On any one pick, how many of the 8,064 ends are lifted?
questions.explain: Three of every four ends are up: 8,064 × 3 ÷ 4 = 6,048.

questions.q: Which side of this drill is the face?
options: The side showing mostly warp, with a clear twill line
questions.explain: A 3/1 twill is warp-faced: the warp floats and the bold diagonal are on the face.

questions.q: Because the warp is finer and much denser than the weft, most of the weight of this cloth is in the warp.
questions.explain: Warp term 128 ÷ 20 = 6.4 against weft 60 ÷ 16 = 3.75: the warp gives about 63% of the weight.

quizzes.case: A buyer sends a sample of a drill and asks the mill to reproduce it. The analysis gives a 3/1 twill, 20 × 16 / 128 × 60, to be woven 63 inches wide. The cloth contracts 8% in length after it leaves the loom, and the warp yarn is 10% longer than the cloth it lies in.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the first four lectures.

questions.q: Which of these needs the fewest heald frames?
questions.explain: Plain weave needs only 2 frames; the 2/1 twill needs 3 and both the others need 4.

questions.q: A twill is written 4/1/1/2. How many squares are filled in one repeat on point paper?
questions.explain: Repeat = 8; each end is up on 4 + 1 = 5 picks: 5 × 8 = 40.

questions.q: Two cloths: A is 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 and B is 20 × 16 / 128 × 60. By the quick rule, how many GSM heavier is B, to the nearest whole number?
questions.explain: B = 253.75 and A = 150; difference = 104 GSM.

questions.q: A weave has a repeat of 16 ends but only 4 different end movements. With a suitable draft it needs
questions.explain: The number of healds equals the number of different end movements, not the number of ends in the repeat.

questions.q: A thin line across the full width of the cloth, where one weft thread is absent, is
questions.explain: Picks run across the cloth, so a missing pick shows as a line across; a missing end shows along the cloth.

questions.q: In a 3/1 twill every pick has three ends lifted for each end left down.
questions.explain: Each pick repeats the 3 up, 1 down order, shifted one end from the pick before.

questions.q: Moving the lifting order one end to the left on each pick instead of to the right changes
options: The twill direction from Z to S
questions.explain: The weave is the same in every other respect; only the direction of the diagonal reverses.

questions.q: A cloth is 63 inches wide with 128 ends per inch, woven as a 3/1 twill on 4 healds, straight draft. How many ends are carried by each heald frame?
questions.explain: 8,064 ends shared equally by 4 frames = 2,016 ends per frame.

questions.q: A tappet loom has 8 frames. Which design can it NOT weave?
options: A cord needing 12 different end movements
questions.explain: Twelve movements need twelve frames, more than the loom has; that design goes to a dobby.

questions.q: The quick GSM rule gives the same answer for a plain weave and a twill of the same counts and threads per inch.
questions.explain: The rule uses only counts and densities; it does not see the weave or the exact crimp.
